---
title: "Walk-Forward Testing with Purging"
subtitle: "Testing only on data the models have not seen"
description: "How the data is split into training, validation and test periods that move forward through time, with gaps that stop overlapping labels leaking information."
toc: true
toc-depth: 2
---

## 1. What problem does it solve?

A model can look excellent on data it has already seen and fail on new data. Walk-forward testing makes
every reported result **out of sample**: the model is trained on the past, tested on the next period it has
never seen, then moved forward and repeated, the way it would be used in practice. Purging removes a
subtler leak that ordinary splits miss.

## 2. What assumptions does it make?

- The recent past is a **reasonable guide** to the period that follows, at least over one test window.
- **Time order** is never broken: nothing from after a forecast date is used to make that forecast.
- Window lengths and the number of windows are **fixed in advance**, so they cannot be tuned to make results
  look better.

## 3. What data does it need?

The dated panel of [indicators](../market-indicators/index.qmd) and labels, the label horizon $h$ (five
sessions), and the chosen window lengths, for example three years of training, six months of validation and
three months of testing.

## 4. How does it work?

Each step splits time into consecutive blocks, separated by gaps:

$$
\underbrace{[\,t_0,\; t_1 - h\,)}_{\text{train}}
\;\;\underbrace{[\,t_1 - h,\; t_1\,)}_{\text{purge gap}}
\;\;\underbrace{[\,t_1,\; t_2 - h\,)}_{\text{validation}}
\;\;\underbrace{[\,t_2 - h,\; t_2\,)}_{\text{purge gap}}
\;\;\underbrace{[\,t_2,\; t_3\,)}_{\text{test}}
$$

The gap matters because the label for day $t$ depends on prices up to day $t + h$. Without a gap, the last
training labels would be built from prices that fall inside the validation or test period, quietly leaking
the future into training. After each step, all boundaries move forward by the length of the test block and
the models are retrained. A final period at the end, the **sealed holdout**, is used once, after every
design decision has been fixed.

## 5. What are its strengths?

- **Honest.** Every reported forecast was made with only the information available at the time.
- **Realistic.** It mirrors how the system would actually be retrained and used.
- **Shows stability.** Results for each step reveal whether performance is consistent or driven by one
  lucky period.

## 6. What are its weaknesses?

- **Less data per model.** Each model only sees the history before its test block.
- **Design choices can still leak.** Repeatedly changing a model after seeing test results is a form of
  overfitting the test periods; the sealed holdout and a record of every trial guard against this.
- **Window lengths involve trade-offs.** Longer training is more stable but slower to adapt, so lengths are
  fixed before testing rather than tuned.

## 7. How could it apply to markets?

It governs every model in the [architecture](../../phd/architecture.html): the forecasters in 02 are trained
and calibrated this way, the recalibration schedule in 08 follows the window boundaries, and every result in
10 comes from the test blocks, the sealed holdout or prospective paper trading.

## 8. What does the Python code look like?

```python
import pandas as pd

def walk_forward_splits(dates, train=756, valid=126, test=63, horizon=5, holdout=252):
    """Yield (train, valid, test) date ranges with purge gaps. The last `holdout` days are sealed.
    dates: sorted unique trading dates."""
    dates = pd.DatetimeIndex(dates)
    usable = dates[:len(dates) - holdout]
    start = 0
    while start + train + valid + test <= len(usable):
        t1 = start + train            # first validation day
        t2 = t1 + valid               # first test day
        yield (usable[start:t1 - horizon],          # train, ending before the first purge gap
               usable[t1:t2 - horizon],             # validation, ending before the second gap
               usable[t2:t2 + test])                # test
        start += test                               # roll forward by one test block

# for train_d, valid_d, test_d in walk_forward_splits(panel.index.unique()):
#     fit on panel.loc[train_d], tune and calibrate on panel.loc[valid_d], forecast panel.loc[test_d]
```

## 9. How are its outputs explained?

Every forecast is stored with the boundaries of the windows used to produce it, so anyone can check that it
used only earlier data. Results are reported per step as well as overall. A hypothetical example:

| Step | Training ends | Test period | Brier score |
|:--:|:--:|:--:|:--:|
| 1 | Dec 2018 | Q1 2019 | 0.2462 |
| 2 | Mar 2019 | Q2 2019 | 0.2471 |
| 3 | Jun 2019 | Q3 2019 | 0.2448 |

: Illustrative values only. {.striped}

A timeline of the windows, with the sealed holdout marked, appears in the testing section of the
[architecture](../../phd/architecture.html), so a reviewer can see at a glance what each model saw and
when.
